images.caption: Figure 1:SFT and RL exhibit significant differences duringmulti-stagetraining. SFT shows task conflicts, which impairs performance, while RL can steadily improve performance across tasks.

Figure 2:Analysis of Parameter Update Dynamics across SFT and RL. The heatmaps display the pairwise cosine similarity (off-diagonal) and theL2L_{2}norm magnitude (diagonal) of parameter update vectors for different tasks. Left: SFT update has a larger absolute similarity value. (≈1.0\approx 1.0). Right: RL updates show near-zero similarity, indicating orthogonal and task-specific parameter adjustments.
Figure 3:Distribution of the score functionSSsampled during training by RL and SFT on different tasks (Math and Science). We use t-SNE to reduce the dimensionality for visualization.

Figure 4:Analysis of RL training on interfering tasks.Top:Distribution of the score functionSSsampled during RL training on math, code and game.Bottom:Corresponding performance comparison on Math (AIME25) and Code (LiveCodeBench) tasks. Training game models in parallel with math or code models can lead to significant performance losses.

Figure 5:The Trade-off between Single-Task Exploration and Multi-Task Coexistence. When rollout temperatureτ\taugrows, we calculates the performance of Math Model, intra-group gradient variance (measured by−log⁡V-\log V), and Naive Parallel-RL accuracy on MATH500. Increasingτ\tauimproves single-task performance but also increases gradient variance, leading to higher gradient interference. As a result, the non-monotonic trend of Parallel-RL performance reveals a sweet spot that balances exploration benefits and interference costs.

Figure 6:Distribution of the score functionSSsampled during training by RL and SFT on different tasks (Math, Code and Logic). We use t-SNE to reduce the dimensionality of the high-dimensional score function vectors for visualization.
